post: It started with questions grandparents ask their grandchildren every day. How do I send a text? How do I fix the volume on this thing? Medha and Reshma Lalani could have answered and moved on. Instead they recognized something larger behind the questions: a digital divide separating an entire generation from the tools modern life now requires. So they built Tech Buddies, connecting high school students with seniors for personalized, 1-on-1 tech help. The initiative has now reached more than 3,500 seniors and grown to over 115 student volunteers, with new chapters forming internationally. This is what civic virtue looks like when a students put it into practice. Responsibility, in seeing a need and claiming it. Respect, in affirming the dignity of people left behind in our rapidly changing world. Meet the 2026 MyImpact Challenge National Grand Prize Winners and hear the story in their own words, alongside a moving reflection from the grandparents who inspired it. 👉  https://bit.ly/3U9e1Ae  #MyImpactChallenge  #CivicsEducation  #StudentLeadership  #CivicVirtue  #BRI

The Founders understood rights as protections. No one may interfere with your speech, your worship, your property. Franklin Roosevelt proposed something different: rights the government must actively provide. His 1944 State of the Union, the "Second Bill of Rights" speech, listed employment, medical care, housing, and economic security among them. Roosevelt died 15 months later, but his successors passed much of the agenda into law. The distinction between negative and positive rights is one of the most consequential ideas in American constitutional debate, and it remains genuinely contested today. BRI's newest Primary Source Essentials makes that distinction clear in just a couple of minutes. John Adams thought Americans would celebrate independence on July 2. That was the day the Second Continental Congress unanimously adopted Richard Henry Lee's resolution declaring the colonies "free and independent states." Adams wrote to Abigail that it was the greatest question ever debated in America. 2 days later, Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, and July 4 became the date we remember. Both days mattered. Understanding why is the beginning of understanding what the Declaration actually did. BRI's newest A250 Mini Documentary walks through the full sequence: the debate, the drafting, and the principles of equality, natural rights, and self-government that Americans have been claiming ever since. Watch it here:  https://bit.ly/45qL59g  #CivicEducation  #AmericanHistory  #A250  #DeclarationOfIndependence

Amber Chih grew up with Tourette syndrome. So she built something to make sure people like her are heard. The Northwood High School student just won the $7,500 grand prize in BRI's MyImpact Challenge for A Thousand Words, an advocacy program amplifying the voices of people with invisible disabilities. She interviewed 50+ people across America, built a storytelling gallery, created a classroom curriculum that's reached 2,500+ students, and partnered with the City of Irvine to launch Invisible Disabilities Awareness Week. Fellow Irvine student Shaili Chudasama of Portola High School took the $5,000 second prize for Startup Stars, teaching 100+ middle schoolers to launch real businesses. This is what happens when students turn personal passion into community impact. Congratulations to both 👇  https://bit.ly/4wmci89  #CivicEducation  #StudentLeadership  #MyImpactChallenge  #Civics

"America's a home. We're an idea. But we also have been, and will continue to be, an argument." That's David Bobb on the 701 Civics podcast, and it's the heart of his new book with Tony Williams, Divided Over the Declaration. His central claim runs against the grain of how we usually talk about our differences: the argument over the Declaration of Independence isn't a sign of national weakness. It's a feature of American life, and always has been. From Frederick Douglass to Abraham Lincoln to Barbara Jordan, generation after generation has returned to the same document to ask the same question: are we living up to the promise that all are created equal? Douglass called the Declaration a promissory note. Lincoln called it the "apple of gold." Jordan, the lowest-ranking member of the Watergate committee, told the nation her faith in the Constitution was "total," even as she named that people like her were left out of it at the founding. The through-line, Bobb argues, is that returning to first principles is how a self-governing people works through its hardest disagreements. As Jordan put it, the task is not the elimination of disagreements, but the management of them. 🎧 Listen here:  https://bit.ly/4xuuNIx  #CivicsEducation  #DeclarationOfIndependence  #AmericanHistory  #CivicDiscourse  #BillOfRightsInstitute

A raccoon named Rebecca arrived at the White House as an ingredient. She was meant for the Thanksgiving dinner. Grace Coolidge adopted her instead. That small act says a lot about the woman. While her husband kept meetings short and words shorter, Grace opened the White House to the public, greeting visitors herself. She was the first First Lady to hold a bachelor's degree, taught at a school for the deaf, and welcomed Helen Keller to the presidential home more than once. When her son died in the summer of 1924, she kept her public appearances and let the country grieve alongside her rather than closing herself off. Respect, in her hands, was not a formality. It was how she treated people. This In Pursuit video is based on an essay by Colleen Shogan and produced with In Pursuit, an initiative of More Perfect.
